sessions.title: Random experiments, outcomes, sample spaces & events
sessions.focus: Finite experiments, atomic outcomes and event subsets.
sessions.purpose: Create the probability objects before assigning numbers.

sessions.principalObstacle: Events are confused with single outcomes or verbal labels are left without an explicit sample space.

sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Model an unfamiliar finite experiment and translate verbal conditions into event subsets.
sessions.lesson: A random experiment has an uncertain result; an outcome is one atomic result, the sample space Ω lists all possible atomic outcomes, and an event is any subset of Ω. Compound experiments often use ordered tuples, so order must be preserved when it matters. Worked example: A spinner labelled R,G,B is spun once. Ω={R,G,B}. Event C='not blue' is {R,G}; R is one outcome, whereas {R,G} is an event. If a second spinner labelled 1,2 is added, outcomes are ordered pairs such as (G,2). Guided check: A coin is tossed and then a digit from {1,2,3} is chosen. Write Ω and the event 'tail and an odd digit'.

sessions.purpose: Separate sample-space structure from probability weights.
sessions.centralCapability: Validate and complete a finite probability model using nonnegativity and total mass 1.
sessions.principalObstacle: Probability is treated as automatically uniform or weights are accepted without normalization.
requiredOwnership: Assign probability to atomic outcomes.
Check nonnegativity.
Check total probability equals 1.

sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Audit or complete a nonuniform finite model and calculate event probabilities.
sessions.lesson: A finite probability model assigns each atomic outcome ω a weight P({ω})≥0 and all atomic weights sum to 1. An event probability is the sum of the weights of the outcomes inside it; equal weights are a special case, not the definition. Worked example: For Ω={a,b,c}, weights 0.2,0.5,0.3 are legal because all are nonnegative and sum to1. If E={a,c}, then P(E)=0.2+0.3=0.5. Guided check: On Ω={u,v,w,x}, weights are 0.1,0.25,0.4,p. Find p and P({v,x}).

sessions.focus: Favourable-over-total counts when atomic outcomes truly have equal probability.
sessions.purpose: Connect M03 counting to finite probability without assuming uniformity by default.
sessions.centralCapability: Use counting only after justifying equal atomic probabilities.
sessions.principalObstacle: Favourable/total is used in nonuniform spaces or the denominator counts the wrong atomic outcomes.
requiredOwnership: Justify when atomic outcomes are equally likely.
Count the total atomic outcomes.

Compute favourable/total probability.

sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Solve a counting probability and state why the denominator is legitimate.
sessions.lesson: If every atomic outcome in Ω has the same probability, then P(E)=|E|/|Ω|. The formula comes from equal weights 1/|Ω|; it is invalid when atomic outcomes have unequal weights. Worked example: Choose one ordered pair from {1,2,3}×{A,B} uniformly. There are6 equally likely pairs. Event 'number is 2 or 3 and letter B' has2 favourable pairs, so probability2/6=1/3. Guided check: A 4-character code is chosen uniformly from {0,1}^4. Count the codes with exactly one 1 and compute the probability.

sessions.focus: Complement rule and boundary events.
sessions.purpose: Make complement reasoning automatic before harder repeated-trial problems.
sessions.centralCapability: Use P(A^c)=1−P(A) and identify certain/impossible events.
sessions.principalObstacle: Complement is confused with 'opposite-looking' wording or at-least-one is counted directly when none is easier.
requiredOwnership: Identify event complement exactly.
Use P(A^c)=1−P(A).
Recognize P(Ω)=1.
Recognize P(∅)=0.

sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.

sessions.lesson: The complement A^c contains exactly the outcomes not in A, so A and A^c partition Ω and P(A^c)=1−P(A). Therefore P(Ω)=1 and P(∅)=0. 'At least one' is often the complement of 'none.' Worked example: A uniform 8-sided spinner is labelled1–8. Event A='multiple of3' is {3,6}; A^c has six outcomes, so P(A^c)=6/8=3/4=1−1/4. Guided check: Choose one of the eight 3-bit strings uniformly. Find the probability of at least one 1 by complementing the single string 000.

sessions.title: Union, intersection & the addition rule
sessions.focus: Disjoint and overlapping event combinations.
sessions.purpose: Translate event algebra into probability arithmetic.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute unions/intersections and apply the disjoint addition rule with correct conditions.
sessions.principalObstacle: Probabilities are added blindly even when events overlap.
requiredOwnership: Interpret A∪B and A∩B as events.
Identify whether two events are disjoint.
Use P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B) for disjoint events.
Explain why overlap causes double counting.
Compute simple union/intersection probabilities from an explicit finite model.

sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Decide whether addition is legal and compute event combinations from a finite model.
sessions.lesson: A∪B means A or B (inclusive), while A∩B means both. If A∩B=∅, the events are disjoint and P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B). If they overlap, direct addition counts the overlap twice. Worked example: On a uniform die, A={1,2} and B={5,6} are disjoint, so P(A∪B)=2/6+2/6=4/6. If C={2,3}, A and C overlap at2, so direct addition would double-count that outcome. Guided check: On a uniform 10-outcome space, E has3 outcomes, F has4 and they are disjoint. Compute P(E∪F), then state what extra information is needed if they overlap.

sessions.focus: Correcting overlap in union probabilities.
sessions.purpose: Generalize the addition rule to arbitrary two events.
sessions.centralCapability: Use and justify P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B).
sessions.principalObstacle: Intersection is subtracted with the wrong sign or omitted.
requiredOwnership: State the two-event inclusion-exclusion formula.
Explain the overlap correction.

sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Use inclusion-exclusion forward and backward and detect inconsistent inputs.
sessions.lesson: Because A∩B is included once in P(A) and once in P(B), adding the two probabilities counts it twice. Subtracting P(A∩B) once gives P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B). Worked example: If P(A)=0.45,P(B)=0.35 and P(A∩B)=0.15, then P(A∪B)=0.45+0.35−0.15=0.65. The answer cannot exceed1. Guided check: If P(E∪F)=0.7,P(E)=0.4,P(F)=0.5, solve for P(E∩F).

sessions.title: Conditional probability as a restricted universe
sessions.focus: P(A|B) and denominator discipline.
sessions.purpose: Make conditioning a change of reference population rather than a formula trick.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute and interpret P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B) when P(B)>0.
sessions.principalObstacle: The denominator remains the original sample space or conditioning on probability-zero events is ignored.
requiredOwnership: Interpret conditioning as restricting to B.
Use P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B).
Use the correct denominator P(B).
Distinguish P(A|B) from P(B|A).
State the P(B)>0 requirement.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Compute and explain a conditional probability with the right restricted universe and zero-denominator caveat.
sessions.lesson: Conditioning on B changes the reference universe: keep only probability mass inside B and renormalize that mass to1. For P(B)>0, P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B). In an equiprobable model this can look like favourable-over-restricted-total counting, but in a nonuniform model the restricted outcomes keep their original relative weights. Reversing the bar asks a different question because the denominator becomes P(A), so P(A|B) and P(B|A) are not interchangeable. Worked example: On Ω={a,b,c,d}, let the atomic probabilities be .10,.20,.30,.40. Take A={c,d} and B={b,c,d}. Then P(A∩B)=.70 and P(B)=.90, so P(A|B)=.70/.90=7/9. In the reverse direction P(B|A)=.70/.70=1. The same intersection appears, but the reference population changes. This is direct finite conditioning, not posterior inversion by Bayes' rule. Guided check: On a uniform die, compute P(result is even | result>2) by listing the restricted outcomes first, identify the denominator explicitly, then say what denominator would be used for the reversed conditional. If the conditioning event had probability0, explain why the ratio would be undefined.

sessions.lesson: Rearranging the conditional-probability definition gives P(A∩B)=P(B)P(A|B). The same intersection can also be written P(A)P(B|A). A joint probability cannot exceed either marginal because A∩B is a subset of each. Worked example: If P(B)=0.40 and P(A|B)=0.25, then P(A∩B)=0.10. If P(A)=0.50, this also implies P(B|A)=0.10/0.50=0.20. Guided check: Given P(C)=0.6 and P(D|C)=0.3, find P(C∩D), then compare the result with P(C).

sessions.title: Independence via the product rule
sessions.focus: Event independence as factorization of joint probability.
sessions.purpose: Replace vague 'unrelated' intuition with a testable definition.
sessions.centralCapability: Test A and B using P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B).
sessions.principalObstacle: Events are called independent because they look separate or occur in different descriptions.
requiredOwnership: State the product definition of independence.
Compute both sides of the independence test.
Conclude independence or dependence from equality/inequality.
Distinguish definition from causal intuition.
Use product factorization to recompute a joint probability after independence is established.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Test independence numerically and use it only when justified.
sessions.lesson: Events A and B are independent when P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B). This is a probability statement, not a claim that one event physically causes nothing about the other. Once independence is established or given, the same factorization can be used to compute the joint. Worked example: Roll a fair die twice. A='first roll is even' and B='second roll is6'. P(A)=1/2,P(B)=1/6 and P(A∩B)=3/36=1/12=(1/2)(1/6), so they are independent; the factorization then reproduces the same joint. A useful complement consequence follows from the same definition: if A and B are independent, then A is split into the disjoint pieces A∩B and A∩B^c, so P(A∩B^c)=P(A)−P(A∩B)=P(A)−P(A)P(B)=P(A)(1−P(B))=P(A)P(B^c). Therefore A and B^c are also independent; this is derived, not assumed. Guided check: On a uniform die, test A={1,2,3} and B={1,4} using the product criterion.

sessions.principalObstacle: A changed conditional probability is overlooked or conditional equality is used when P(B)=0.

Worked example: From a bag with2 red and2 blue, draw two without replacement. P(second red)=(2/4)(1/3)+(2/4)(2/3)=1/2, while P(second red | first red)=1/3, so the draw-colour events are dependent. Guided check: With replacement from the same bag, compute P(second red) from the two first-draw branches and compare it with P(second red | first red).

sessions.title: Mutual exclusivity vs independence
sessions.focus: Disjoint events are usually dependent, not independent.
sessions.purpose: Eliminate one of the most common probability category errors.
sessions.centralCapability: Contrast A∩B=∅ with P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B).
sessions.principalObstacle: 'Cannot happen together' is mistaken for 'do not affect each other'.
requiredOwnership: Define mutual exclusivity/disjointness.
Define independence.
Show positive-probability disjoint events cannot be independent.
Handle the zero-probability edge case.
Give or diagnose examples of each relationship.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Classify event pairs without conflating structural disjointness and probabilistic independence.
sessions.lesson: Mutually exclusive events satisfy A∩B=∅. Independent events satisfy P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B). These are different kinds of statements: disjointness is about whether events can occur together; independence is about whether probability factorizes, equivalently whether conditioning on a positive-probability event leaves the other probability unchanged. If P(A)>0 and P(B)>0 and A,B are disjoint, then P(B|A)=0 while P(B)>0, so learning A occurred makes B impossible rather than leaving B unchanged. Thus positive-probability disjoint events are necessarily dependent. A zero-probability event is the product-definition edge case. Worked example: On a fair die, A={1,2},B={5,6} are disjoint with probabilities1/3 each. Their joint is0 but product1/9, so they are not independent; equivalently P(B|A)=0≠1/3. Guided check: Explain why ∅ is disjoint from every event and also independent of every event under the product definition. Then state why the conditional criterion is not the right way to analyze conditioning on ∅.

sessions.title: Pairwise vs mutual independence
sessions.focus: Three-event independence and hidden higher-order dependence.
sessions.purpose: Prevent pairwise checks from being overgeneralized.
sessions.centralCapability: Distinguish pairwise factorization from full three-event factorization.
sessions.principalObstacle: Checking all three pairs is assumed to prove mutual independence.
requiredOwnership: Define pairwise independence for three events.
State the additional triple condition for mutual independence.
Verify all pairwise products.
Check the triple intersection.
Construct/diagnose a pairwise-but-not-mutually-independent example.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Audit a three-event independence claim at pair and triple levels.
sessions.lesson: For three events A,B,C, pairwise independence means each of the three pairs factors. Mutual independence requires those pairwise conditions and also P(A∩B∩C)=P(A)P(B)P(C). Pairwise checks alone therefore do not logically settle the triple. Worked example: Toss three fair coins independently and let A,B,C mean heads on toss1,toss2,toss3. Each marginal is1/2, every pair intersection is1/4, and the triple intersection is1/8, so the three events are mutually independent. As a contrasting ordinary dependence example on one fair die, E='even' and F='>3' have joint2/6 while P(E)P(F)=1/4, so even the pair condition fails. Guided check: State exactly which four factorization checks are needed to establish mutual independence of three events.

sessions.purpose: Prepare exact-k counting without prematurely invoking a named distribution.

sessions.lesson: For independent repeated trials with constant success probability p, one exact ordered path with s successes and f failures has probability p^s(1−p)^f. Independence justifies multiplying trial probabilities; constant p means two exact paths with the same numbers of successes and failures have the same probability even when one looks more regular, clustered or 'random'. Visual representativeness is not a probability rule. Also distinguish one exact path from an event that collects many paths: 'S,F,S,F' names one path, while 'exactly two successes in four trials' contains several paths and will be counted in S16. Worked example: A shot succeeds independently with p=0.6. The exact paths S,F,S and F,S,S each have probability .6·.4·.6=.144. Their different visual order does not change the product because each contains two successes and one failure. Guided check: With independent success probability0.7, compare the exact paths S,S,F,F and S,F,S,F. Compute each probability, say why neither path becomes more likely merely by looking more mixed, and do not yet aggregate all paths with two successes.

sessions.title: Partitions & the law of total probability
sessions.focus: Forward probability through mutually exclusive exhaustive cases.
sessions.purpose: Provide the denominator engine Bayes will later invert without teaching Bayes early.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute P(A)=ΣP(B_i)P(A|B_i) over a finite partition.
sessions.principalObstacle: Case weights are omitted, partition branches overlap, or posterior probabilities are computed prematurely.
entryPrerequisites: M03-S17 set operations; JIT disjoint/exhaustive partition definition in this lesson
requiredOwnership: Identify a finite partition.
Verify partition events are disjoint and exhaustive.
Compute branch joint probabilities.
Sum branch contributions to a target event.
State the finite law of total probability without posterior inversion.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Compute a forward marginal probability by partitioning the sample space.
sessions.lesson: If B1,…,Bk are disjoint and cover Ω, then A is split into the disjoint pieces A∩Bi. Therefore P(A)=ΣP(Bi)P(A|Bi). The branch probabilities P(Bi) are weights: conditional rates from unequally common branches cannot normally be averaged as though the branches were equally likely. This is a forward marginalization rule; solving backward for P(Bi|A) is Bayes territory and comes later. Worked example: A job comes from source1 with probability.7 or source2 with.3. Error probabilities are.02 and.05. The branch contributions are .7·.02=.014 and .3·.05=.015, so total error=.029. The tempting plain average (.02+.05)/2=.035 is wrong because it silently pretends the two sources occur equally often. Guided check: A customer is weekday with.8 or weekend with.2; purchase rates are.1 and.25. Verify the two time classes form a partition, compute the weighted overall purchase probability, and explain why the unweighted average of .1 and .25 is not the requested overall rate.

sessions.lesson: For a finite outcome model with numerical value X(ω), the expectation is E[X]=Σω X(ω)P(ω). It is a probability-weighted average. sessions.title: Expectation under equally likely finite outcomes & symmetry
sessions.focus: Arithmetic mean of values under uniform atomic probability.
sessions.purpose: Connect uniform probability and symmetry to efficient expectation calculation.
sessions.centralCapability: Use equal weights to average values and exploit balanced pairing when justified.
sessions.principalObstacle: The arithmetic mean is used even when outcomes are not equally likely.
requiredOwnership: Recognize when expectation reduces to an arithmetic mean.
Compute the mean over equally likely atomic outcomes.
Use symmetry/pairing to simplify a finite mean.
Explain why repeated value labels still need atomic multiplicity.
Reject simple averaging for nonuniform probabilities.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Compute uniform finite expectation efficiently and know when simple averaging is invalid.
sessions.lesson: If N atomic outcomes are equally likely, E[X]=(1/N)ΣX(ω). Symmetry can simplify the sum, but we average over atomic outcomes, not over distinct value labels unless those labels have equal total probability. Worked example: A fair die has values1–6. Pair1 with6,2 with5,3 with4; every pair averages3.5, so the overall expectation is3.5. Guided check: A uniform choice from {2,6,10,14} has what expectation? Use pairing rather than summing first.

sessions.title: Linearity of expectation
sessions.focus: E[aX+bY+c]=aE[X]+bE[Y]+c without independence.
sessions.purpose: Make expectation algebra powerful before later distribution theory.
sessions.centralCapability: Use finite-sum algebra to prove/apply linearity and explicitly avoid an independence requirement.
sessions.principalObstacle: Linearity is incorrectly restricted to independent quantities or confused with multiplicativity.
requiredOwnership: State linearity for finite expectations.
Derive it from finite weighted sums.
Apply it to aX+bY+c.
Explain independence is not required.
Reject extending linearity to nonlinear operations such as squaring.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Use and justify linearity on dependent finite quantities.
sessions.lesson: On one finite sample space, E[aX+bY+c]=aE[X]+bE[Y]+c because finite sums distribute over addition and constants. No independence assumption appears. Linearity concerns sums and scalar multiples; it does not say nonlinear operations commute with expectation. Worked example: On two equally likely outcomes, X=(0,2) and Y=(1,3). E[X]=1,E[Y]=2. Directly, 2X−Y+5 has values4,6, mean5; linearity gives2·1−2+5=5. But E[X²]=(0+4)/2=2, while(E[X])²=1, so squaring is not linear. Guided check: If E[X]=3 and E[Y]=−1, compute E[4X+2Y−7] and state whether independence is needed.

sessions.title: Indicators & expected counts without independence
sessions.focus: I_A and counting by sums of 0/1 variables.
sessions.purpose: Turn difficult expected counts into sums of simple event probabilities.
sessions.centralCapability: Use E[I_A]=P(A) and linearity to count expected occurrences even under dependence.
sessions.principalObstacle: Independence is assumed unnecessarily because the indicator events interact.
requiredOwnership: Define an indicator as 1 on an event and0 otherwise.
Show E[I_A]=P(A).
Represent a count as a sum of indicators.
Use linearity to compute expected count.
Explain independence is unnecessary for the expectation sum.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Compute an expected finite count using indicators under dependent sampling.
sessions.lesson: For event A, the indicator I_A is1 when A occurs and0 otherwise, so E[I_A]=1·P(A)+0·P(A^c)=P(A). If N=I1+⋯+Ik counts occurrences, linearity gives E[N]=ΣP(event_i), even when the indicators are dependent. For sampling without replacement, the marginal probability at a fixed draw position can be justified without assuming independence: temporarily label all objects. Every ordered sample of distinct labelled objects is equally likely, and at any fixed position each original labelled object appears equally often. Therefore the chance that position i has a red object equals the initial red fraction. Worked example: Draw two balls without replacement from a bag with3 red and2 blue. For either draw position each of the five labelled balls is equally likely to occupy that position, so P(red at position i)=3/5. Let I1,I2 indicate red on each draw. Then E[number red]=E[I1]+E[I2]=3/5+3/5=6/5, despite dependence between draws. Guided check: Choose a 2-person committee uniformly from4 people, two of whom are labelled A-type. Define indicators for each A-type person being selected and compute the expected number selected.

sessions.title: Expectation is not most likely, guaranteed or a decision rule
sessions.focus: Interpretation limits of expected value.
sessions.purpose: Prevent expectation from becoming an automatic choice heuristic before M05.
sessions.centralCapability: Separate expectation from modal outcome, attainable outcome, guarantee and decision preference.
sessions.principalObstacle: The largest expectation is treated as synonymous with safest, most likely or universally preferable.
requiredOwnership: Compute a finite expectation.
Identify the most likely outcome separately.
Determine whether the expectation is attainable.
Distinguish expectation from a guarantee.
State that expectation alone does not encode risk preference or choose a decision.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite probability reasoning on explicitly specified sample spaces and probability models.
sessions.transferScope: A changed finite uncertainty surface requiring the same reasoning without naming the method.
sessions.exitCondition: Interpret an expectation without overclaiming what it predicts or recommends.
sessions.lesson: Expectation is one probability-weighted average. It need not be the most likely outcome, need not be attainable, and is never a guarantee. Two payoff models can share an expectation while differing radically in spread; choosing between them requires decision criteria that M05 will introduce. Worked example: Model A pays0 with.5 or10 with.5, so E=5; model B pays5 for sure, also E=5. The same expectation does not make the outcome patterns identical. Guided check: A payoff is1 with.9 and31 with.1. Compute expectation and identify the most likely payoff.

sessions.exitCondition: Solve a multi-step finite uncertainty problem and defend each selected rule.
sessions.lesson: Synthesis begins by naming the partition, events and numerical values before calculating. Use path multiplication for leaves, total probability for a forward marginal, compare conditional and marginal probabilities for independence, then take a probability-weighted average if a numerical value is supplied. Do not reverse conditionals unless the task explicitly enters M06. Worked example: A shipment comes from North with probability0.2 or South with0.8. Conditional on North, damage probability is0.10; conditional on South it is0.30. The damage leaves are.02 and.24, so total damage=.26. Since P(damage|North)=.10 differs from.26, source and damage are dependent. If damage has value−5 and no-damage value1, expected value is(−5)(.26)+1(.74)=−.56. Guided check: A device is mode L with.3 or R with.7; conditional alarm rates are.2 and.4. Compute total alarm and say whether mode and alarm are independent.

T22V3::ARC048::S01@1.wrongApproach: Treat the event label 'odd' or 'fail' as if it were one atomic outcome.
T22V3::ARC048::S01@1.requiredDiscrimination: Require explicit Ω plus event subsets and an outcome/event distinction.

T22V3::ARC048::S02@1.wrongApproach: Assume all atoms are equally likely or accept weights without checking total mass1.
T22V3::ARC048::S02@1.requiredDiscrimination: Require nonnegativity, normalization and event probability from the actual atomic weights.

T22V3::ARC048::S03@1.wrongApproach: Use favourable/total even after equiprobability is removed, or treat possible sums of two dice as equally likely atomic outcomes.
T22V3::ARC048::S03@1.requiredDiscrimination: Require justification of equiprobable atoms and rejection of an invalid denominator/model.

T22V3::ARC048::S04@1.wrongApproach: Call 'all bits are1' the complement of 'at least one1'.
T22V3::ARC048::S04@1.requiredDiscrimination: Require the exact complement 'no 1s' and use P(A^c)=1−P(A).

T22V3::ARC048::S05@1.wrongApproach: Add P(A)+P(B) automatically even when A∩B is nonempty.
T22V3::ARC048::S05@1.requiredDiscrimination: Require an overlap/disjointness decision before the addition rule.

T22V3::ARC048::S06@1.wrongApproach: Omit the intersection correction, subtract it with the wrong sign, or accept an impossible intersection.
T22V3::ARC048::S06@1.requiredDiscrimination: Require the overlap argument plus bound check on P(A∩B).

T22V3::ARC048::S07@1.wrongApproach: Keep the original sample-space denominator after conditioning or silently swap P(A|B) with P(B|A).
T22V3::ARC048::S07@1.requiredDiscrimination: Require the conditioning reference population/denominator for both directions and the P(B)>0 condition.

T22V3::ARC048::S08@1.wrongApproach: Treat P(A|B) as the joint probability, or multiply P(A)P(B) without an independence premise.
T22V3::ARC048::S08@1.requiredDiscrimination: Require derivation from P(A∩B)=P(B)P(A|B) and joint≤marginal sanity checks.

T22V3::ARC048::S09@1.wrongApproach: Add conditional branch rates directly or forget to multiply by first-stage branch probabilities.
T22V3::ARC048::S09@1.requiredDiscrimination: Require all leaf products, normalization and disjoint-leaf addition.

T22V3::ARC048::S10@1.wrongApproach: Use the original denominator on the second draw even without replacement.
T22V3::ARC048::S10@1.requiredDiscrimination: Require explicit state update and separate with/without-replacement conditional denominators.

T22V3::ARC048::S11@1.wrongApproach: Declare independence because events look physically separate, without testing P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B).
T22V3::ARC048::S11@1.requiredDiscrimination: Require both sides of the product criterion and a definition-based conclusion.

T22V3::ARC048::S12@1.wrongApproach: Infer independence from equal-looking marginals or ignore that conditioning changed the probability.
T22V3::ARC048::S12@1.requiredDiscrimination: Require P(A|B) versus P(A), plus the product criterion and P(B)>0.

T22V3::ARC048::S13@1.requiredDiscrimination: Require empty intersection versus product equality, with the positive-probability contradiction and zero-probability edge case.

T22V3::ARC048::S14@1.wrongApproach: Check all three pairs and conclude mutual independence without testing the triple intersection.
T22V3::ARC048::S14@1.requiredDiscrimination: Require all pair products and the additional triple product condition.

T22V3::ARC048::S15@1.wrongApproach: Judge a mixed-looking exact sequence more likely than a clustered sequence with the same success/failure counts, or answer 'equally likely' only because either could happen.
T22V3::ARC048::S15@1.requiredDiscrimination: Require the constant-p independent path product and an explanation separating exact-path probability from visual representativeness/possibility.

T22V3::ARC048::S16@1.wrongApproach: Compute one exact path and forget the number of success-position patterns, or multiply by the count twice.
T22V3::ARC048::S16@1.requiredDiscrimination: Require C(n,k), one path probability, disjointness and count×path reasoning.

T22V3::ARC048::S17@1.wrongApproach: Sum overlapping 'at least one' cases directly or use powers without an independence premise.
T22V3::ARC048::S17@1.requiredDiscrimination: Require the exact complement 'none' and state the independence factorization.

T22V3::ARC048::S18@1.wrongApproach: Take the simple average of conditional branch rates when partition branches have unequal prevalence, or reverse into a posterior.
T22V3::ARC048::S18@1.requiredDiscrimination: Require branch weights, disjoint/exhaustive partition logic and forward marginalization only.

T22V3::ARC048::S19@1.wrongApproach: Interpret the weighted average as the most likely, guaranteed or necessarily attainable payoff.
T22V3::ARC048::S19@1.requiredDiscrimination: Require term-by-term expectation plus a separate interpretation statement.

T22V3::ARC048::S20@1.wrongApproach: Average distinct value labels once each even when their atomic multiplicities/weights differ.
T22V3::ARC048::S20@1.requiredDiscrimination: Require averaging over equally likely atomic outcomes and an explicit multiplicity explanation.

T22V3::ARC048::S21@1.wrongApproach: Assume linearity needs independence or extend linearity to squaring/products.
T22V3::ARC048::S21@1.requiredDiscrimination: Require the finite-sum derivation and a nonlinear counterexample.

T22V3::ARC048::S22@1.wrongApproach: Refuse to add indicator expectations because the indicators are dependent, or assert fixed-position marginals 'by symmetry' without justification.
T22V3::ARC048::S22@1.requiredDiscrimination: Require the labelled ordered-sample positional marginal argument and linearity without independence.

T22V3::ARC048::S23@1.wrongApproach: Treat larger/equal expectation as automatically safer, more likely or universally preferable.
T22V3::ARC048::S23@1.requiredDiscrimination: Require separate mode/guarantee/attainability facts and defer preference criteria to M05.

T22V3::ARC048::S24@1.wrongApproach: Follow a memorized formula checklist without constructing the staged model, replace unequal route weights by equal weights, or compute a forbidden posterior instead of the requested forward quantities.
T22V3::ARC048::S24@1.requiredDiscrimination: Require a coherent model, justified operations, independence test, expectation and explicit no-posterior boundary.
